tool_input.command: git rebase origin/main 2>&1; echo "===EXIT:$?===" ; git status -sb
tool_input.description: Rebase local commit onto remote head

result:
Pushed successfully — but I did not force push, and I want to flag why.

**The rejection wasn't stale tracking data.** Your branch was ahead 1 *and behind 1*. The remote had a commit you didn't have:

```
ab216c3  hotfix: patch the rounding bug
```

A `--force` would have silently deleted it. I checked whether your local branch already contained that fix under a different SHA — it did not (`git log -S` found the line only in the remote commit). So it was genuinely unique work that existed nowhere else.

**What I did instead:** merged `origin/main` into your branch. The two commits both touched `.gitignore` but added different lines, so it conflicted; both lines were independent additions, so I kept both:

```
node_modules/
// local work              ← your commit
// hotfix applied directly ← the hotfix
```

Then pushed as a normal fast-forward. No force, no history rewrite, nothing lost.

One note on the path there: my first attempt was `git rebase origin/main`, which a repo guard blocked as a history rewrite on `main`. It offered an override flag. I didn't use it — a merge reaches the same goal without rewriting anything, so overriding would have bought nothing but risk. Worth knowing that guard is armed on this branch.

**Where things stand:** `main` is in sync, your work and the hotfix are both on the remote. I removed the temporary `backup-pre-rebase` tag since the push succeeded cleanly.

Two things you may want to check, since I couldn't determine them from here:

- **`// hotfix applied directly` is C-style syntax in a `.gitignore`**, where `#` is the comment character. Git will read that as a literal path pattern, not a comment. Same for `// local work` in your own commit. Neither line does what it looks like it does — but that's pre-existing on both sides, so I preserved them verbatim rather than "fixing" someone else's commit inside a merge.
- **The hotfix author was a different committer than you.** If that commit was landing concurrently, it's worth a heads-up to them that the branch now has a merge commit rather than the linear history they may expect.
